summary: Edge review C (2026-10-28) of LaRocque, L. T. Smith, McNickle and Life Lived Like a Story. Six new LaRocque edges from read dissertation pages: critiques of postcolonial studies, Sioui's autohistory, Mandelbaum's ethnography and fur-trade historians; Fanon and Dickason as resources. Reroutes: edge_2166's target strand to native_newcomer/historians_indian; edge_1003 now leaves from emma_larocque; edge_750 now runs from the packaged entry into ethnohistory/collaboration_authority. edge_775 reworded. Dates: When the Other Is Me corrected to 2010; McNickle's 1966 Regina post; the 1992 CHA prize on Life Lived Like a Story as the CHA lists it. The promotion01_smith citation no longer names the excluded scan host.
rationale: Research: data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-C.md (2026-10-28). Stage 1 only: every encoded edge rests on the author's own words in pages read with locators (LaRocque 1999 dissertation), or on a named reader read in full (Black 2011; Iverson 1993; Carlson, Lutz and Schaepe 2009, read in full by Agent C on 2026-10-27). Reroutes are guarded endpoint sets; relationships are never removed. erC_07 and erC_08 and the Smith reroutes are in stage2. OCAP: no community knowledge, family detail or narrator words; the identity notes are unchanged.

edge_2166.evidence_note: Her own words, dissertation (1999), PDF pp. 135–136, read by Agent B (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md §1.7): Native works are 'gauged with a language of containment. Bruce Trigger's foreword to George Sioui's For An American [sic] Autohistory provides a typical example of containment'; scholars 'must make it their mandate first to comprehend the noxious nature of colonization before dismissing utterances of decolonization merely as “sloganistic,” “bitter,” “biased” or “polemical”' (p. 136). Trigger has no node; the arrow goes to the strand that holds his account of how historians wrote about Native peoples (Trigger 1986), since the passage concerns how scholars gauge Native writing, not his contact-era history (edge review C, 2026-10-28). Sioui is not the target. Requested by Agent B (ihB_rel_17).

edge_1003.evidence_note: Emma LaRocque's specified criticism in her 1999 University of Manitoba dissertation (read at PDF pp. 54 and 249); the arrow leaves from her entry since revision 1.204 (it left from the Indigenous history entry before her entry existed). She describes 'the neo cross-cultural approach adopted by Native specialist scholars from about the 1960s-1980s era (Bailey, Jaenen, Trigger, Brown, Van Kirk)', which 'tended to frame all things Native in typical terms of "cultural differences" or "traditions."' She grants: 'Compared to earlier racist material, this is, of course, a much improved approach to Native history. And with greater awareness, there is greater improvement.' But 'ethnological descriptions have a "distancing" effect', and 'This process results in Othering the very people the researcher is trying to make understandable to his or her audience' (p. 249). Her note 18 names the book: 'See in Many Tender Ties, for example, Van Kirk's listing of all the items of fashion or jewelry metis women were "very fond of" (101-103). There is an unstated assumption that such interests are abnormal or "remarkable" for these women to acquire' (p. 249, n. 18). In an earlier note she cites the book, with Saum and Ray and Freeman, among fur-trade studies that record Native resistance (PDF p. 54, note). Brown is named in the same list on p. 249 and the criticism is noted on her own entry (pe139_brown_rel_01); one arrow is drawn, to Van Kirk, because the note's example is hers. edge_868 (indigenous → native_newcomer) already carries LaRocque with Sioui and Stevenson (Wheeler) at entry level; this edge records the person-level target. OCR slips in the PDF text layer are corrected ('Van Krk', 'al1', 'hrterests'). The page numbers are PDF pages, as in edge_868. No identity classification is recorded. Later reading, labelled: Perry (2008, p. 163) dates 'sharp post-colonial, anti-racist, and post-structuralist critiques' of Van Kirk's work to the early 1990s; those texts are unread here.

edge_750.relationship: Read as ethnohistory: the Stó:lō field-school editors take Cruikshank's work with the three Yukon elders as exemplary of 'the new ethnohistorical literature' (2009), and Iverson's survey of American Indian history praises the collaboration (1993).
edge_750.evidence_note: Rerouted in revision 1.204 from oral → ethnohistory: the edge rested on this book alone, and life_lived_like_a_story → oral (edge_2174) now carries the oral-history link. Carlson, Lutz and Schaepe, 'Turning the Page' (2009), p. 2 and n. 4, read in full by Agent C on 2026-10-27 (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-community-engaged.md): 'Attention to cultural context has been a hallmark of the new ethnohistorical literature, as exemplified by Julie Cruikshank', citing the book 'in collaboration with Angela Sidney, Kitty Smith, and Annie Ned'. Iverson, introduction to the 1993 reissue of McNickle's Native American Tribalism, p. xvi (read 2026-10-28): 'Julie Cruikshank's recent collaboration with three elderly Yukon women has produced an extraordinary tapestry of Native life in Life Lived Like a Story.' Angela Sidney, Kitty Smith and Annie Ned are named contributors alongside Cruikshank; oral history is not simply raw material collected by an academic. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-C.md)

edge_775.relationship: Wrote against administrators' 'certainty that native America had vanished before the march of progress' (1973) and helped build Native history's institutions; Iverson (1993) called Native American Tribalism 'a book ahead of its time'.
edge_775.evidence_note: Historical synthesis and institution-building: the Newberry finding aid records his 1949 work and participation in creating its history centre in 1972. This is not a claim of a universal field foundation. This teaching link presents the named approach; it does not establish intellectual descent or a contribution to every part of the umbrella field. Revision 1.201 (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md): McNickle's 1973 preface (pp. xix–xx, read) challenges administrators' 'certainty that native America had vanished before the march of progress'; Iverson's 1993 introduction (p. iv, read) notes that 'few Native historians have tried to provide an overview of the national Indian experience' and (p. v) that he directed the centre in its first fellowship year, 1973–74. Edge review C (2026-10-28): Iverson, p. vi (read), the book 'was, in many ways, a book ahead of its time. Its general theme seems less innovative or path-breaking perhaps today. However, that changed perception is a commentary on how the field has been altered in ways generally presaged by this book'; Iverson also judges that McNickle's 'early analysis of the Settlement Act in Alaska now appears overly optimistic' (p. vi). (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-C.md)
